title: Choose Kubernetes vs managed application hosting
description: Evaluate whether to adopt Kubernetes or use a managed platform like AWS ECS, Azure App Service, or Google Cloud Run for a greenfield SaaS product.

data.text: Your team is deploying a new SaaS platform. The CTO wants you to choose between a managed container platform (AWS ECS, Azure App Service) and self-managed Kubernetes. The team has one DevOps engineer and five backend developers. The product needs blue/green deployments, autoscaling, and multi-region failover within the next year.

terms.definition: An open-source container orchestration platform for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications.
A cloud provider platform that abstracts infrastructure operations (ECS, App Service, Cloud Run).
The Kubernetes component that manages the cluster state, scheduling, and API server.
A release strategy that keeps the old version running while the new version is validated, then switches traffic.

data.title: Kubernetes is not free
data.text: Kubernetes reduces infrastructure flexibility in exchange for operational control. You must manage etcd backups, certificate rotation, node pool upgrades, and network policies. A managed service absorbs these costs for a premium.

cards.title: Managed Platform (ECS / App Service)
cards.description: Cloud provider manages the control plane; you define tasks or applications.
pros: No control plane to patch, backup, or upgrade
Built-in load balancing and rolling deployments
Lower operational overhead for small teams
Tighter integration with provider IAM, monitoring, and secrets
cons: Vendor lock-in to proprietary APIs and configuration formats
Less flexibility in networking, ingress, and custom operators
Scaling costs can be unpredictable with managed components
Debugging platform issues requires support tickets

cards.title: Self-Managed Kubernetes
cards.description: Full control over cluster configuration, networking, and scheduling.
pros: Rich ecosystem of operators, ingress controllers, and service meshes
Fine-grained control over scheduling, affinity, and resource limits
cons: High operational burden: etcd, API server, node management
Steep learning curve for developers without platform experience
Security surface area is large; misconfiguration is common
Upgrades are manual and potentially disruptive

data.title: Kubernetes: Rolling update with resource limits
data.content: A deployment manifest expressing desired state.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: checkout-api
          image: checkout-api:v2.3.1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }

items.text: Does your team have someone with Kubernetes Day 2 operations experience?
Are your workloads stateful, requiring persistent volumes and operators?
Do you need to run on multiple clouds or on-premises?
Is cost predictability more important than infrastructure flexibility?
Will your team size grow enough to justify a dedicated platform team?

data.caption: Operational effort increases with platform responsibility
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Managed Service] -->|Low control| B[Low ops burden]
    C[Self-Managed K8s] -->|High control| D[High ops burden]
    B --> E[Small team: 1-5 engineers]
    D --> F[Platform team: 10+ engineers]
    E --> G[Faster time to market]
    F --> H[Long-term flexibility]

data.title: Recommended approach: Managed platform now, Kubernetes later
data.content: Start with a managed platform. Your team needs to ship product, not manage etcd clusters. Design your application with the Twelve-Factor App methodology so the migration to Kubernetes later is a configuration change, not an architecture rewrite.

data.title: Migration path
data.text: Containerize everything from day one. Use Docker Compose locally. When you outgrow the managed platform, your Docker images and environment-based configuration make the Kubernetes migration straightforward.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Managed platforms are optimal until team size or compliance requirements force self-management.
Container-first design keeps migration options open.
Kubernetes complexity is a team problem, not just an infrastructure problem.
data.takeaway: Start managed, stay portable, graduate to Kubernetes when you have the team to operate it.
